source.title: How Does Topology of Neural Architectures Impact Gradient Propagation and Model Performance
source.authors: K. Bhardwaj; Gui-Hong Li; R. Marculescu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary text are present; some figure contents are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains networks and reports training-convergence outcomes, but does not test the claim versions’ specified CIFAR error, residual-shortcut, initialization, learning-rate, or normalization comparisons.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy, initial Jacobian singular values, and training-convergence curves. Only the training-convergence results bear directly on training behavior; the test-accuracy and initialization measurements do not measure training classification error. Cited results, including the Wide-ResNet paper’s accuracy and parameter counts, are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study tests how concatenation-type skip topology predicts gradient properties, training convergence and test accuracy. It does not test any specified version: its convergence comparisons vary topology rather than initialization, normalization or identity shortcuts, and do not establish near-zero CIFAR training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the convergence experiments. The broader conclusion is that NN-Mass links topology to layerwise gradient properties, identifies networks with similar test accuracy despite different sizes and depths, and enables direct design of compressed networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies random DenseNet-type skip-connection topologies and compares their training convergence; it does not apply the original claim’s CIFAR training-error recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: For the MNIST MLP examples, similar NN-Mass is associated with similar convergence, while the model with higher NN-Mass converges faster than a deeper, similar-parameter model.

fits_no_version.finding: For the tested MNIST ELU MLPs, X and Y have similar width and NN-Mass and nearly coinciding training-convergence curves despite different depths. Higher-NN-Mass Z converges faster than Y. Figure 4 reports analogous comparisons for two further model groups.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed width in the tested concatenation-skip MLPs, similar NN-Mass predicts similar training convergence, while higher NN-Mass can accompany faster convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial layerwise Jacobian mean singular values correlate more strongly with NN-Mass than parameter count on MNIST: R² = 0.79 versus 0.31.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concatenation-skip topology predicts initial layerwise gradient-propagation properties under a shared initialization scheme.

record.problems: The training-convergence outcomes are shown in a figure without exact endpoint values in the supplied text. The paper reports no training-error endpoint for these examples.
record.rows_left_out: Test-accuracy measurements, initial Jacobian singular-value measurements, and compressed-model test accuracies were left out because they do not measure training classification error or convergence. The Wide-ResNet accuracy and parameter-count data are explicitly taken from the cited paper, with no training performed here.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero CIFAR-10/100 training classification error, including random or corrupted labels, and its dependence on size, stopping or regularization.
Spurious minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student training and their reduction through extra student neurons.
Depth-related training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized CNNs versus identity-residual CNNs, longer-training controls, and special-initialization or Fixup results.
Effects of changing initialization on training speed and trainable depth, including activation matching, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and very deep plain convolutional networks.
Loss recovery, curvature evolution and divergence relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Training-speed and learning-rate-tolerance comparisons with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Section 4.3's no-shortcut depth discussion concerns gradient attenuation and test-accuracy clusters, not the training-error comparison required by V3. Shared initialization and batch normalization are setup choices, not tests of V4 or V6. No additional result bearing on a specified version requires a missing-row entry.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus identity-residual batch-normalized CNNs, depth effects on training error, and the cited special-initialization or Fixup comparisons.
Comparisons of activation-matched initializations, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, and training depth under those initializations.
Learning rates above stability thresholds, loss rises and recovery, sharpness behavior, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons without normalization.

rows.subject: Model X
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST; training accuracy plotted against epochs.
rows.value: Training convergence nearly coincides with Model Y (figure only for numeric values).
rows.note: The paper explicitly says the curves nearly coincide; no endpoint training error is stated.
rows.check: The relative MNIST convergence result is accurately reported, but measures none of V1–V6. Its state cannot be interpreted as observing a claim version.

rows.subject: Model Y
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST; training accuracy plotted against epochs.
rows.value: Training convergence nearly coincides with Model X; Model Z converges significantly faster (figure only for numeric values).
rows.note: The text reports relative convergence, not whether training error reaches zero.
rows.check: Similar convergence to X and slower convergence than Z do not constitute partial evidence for any version. The comparison varies concatenation topology in ELU MLPs.

rows.subject: Model Z
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST; training accuracy plotted against epochs.
rows.value: Training convergence is significantly faster than Model Y (figure only for numeric values).
rows.note: The text attributes the faster convergence to higher NN-Mass and better LDI; it does not state final training error.
rows.check: Faster convergence with higher NN-Mass measures none of V1–V6. Z has 8.3K parameters versus Y's 9.0K; the figure caption's same-parameter description is approximate and conflicts with these stated counts.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
